newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Global workers' body hits SKorean labour law.
newsitem.headline: Global workers' body hits SKorean labour law.

text.p: The major global worker union grouping, the ICFTU, on Wednesday issued a stern condemnation of South Korea's new labour legislation, saying it worsened existing violations of international labour law in the country.

At the same time, the United Nations International Labour Organisation (ILO) in Geneva said it was asking the Seoul government to respond to a formal complaint lodged with it by the Brussels-based ICFTU at the end of last month.

The ICFTU, the International Confederation of Free Trade Unions, said an examination of the new law -- which has sparked massive strikes across South Korea -- showed it "failed to correct the wrongs of the old laws."

The study, an ICFTU statement said, concluded that the legislation "not only failed to take account of proposals repeatedly made by the....ILO to redress existing breaches of international conventions in the labour laws, but even adds new violations of internationally-recognised trade union rights."

Last year the ILO's Committee on Freedom of Association -- which links employers, governments and unions -- called on Seoul to recognise the banned Korean Confederation of Trade Unions (KCTU) and other worker and professional groups.
The Committee also asked Seoul to register unions representing auto-workers, subway employees and a federation of unions in the giant Hyundai industrial group.
Under the new legislation, the KCTU would only be recognised from the year 2000 and the sectoral groupings from 2002.

ILO sources and diplomats said the Committee would almost certainly support the ICFTU position at its next scheduled meeting in March. But the U.N. body has no power to compel South Korea to amend the law.

The ICFTU said it would be sending an international delegation -- including officials of the Trade Union Advisory Committee (TUAC) to the OECD industrialised powers' club -- to Seoul on January 11 to voice concern over the law.

South Korea has just joined the 29-member OECD, the Organisation for Economic Cooperation and Development, but the TUAC last week accused Seoul of violating pledges on labour law made when it was seeking admission.
The ICFTU study listed five areas in which it said the legislation added to current violations of union rights.

These included provision for replacement of strikers by outside workers "as temporarily-employed strike breakers," for dismissed workers to lose the right to belong to a union, and for a ban on companies paying strikers during a stoppage.
The others were a ban to be implemented by stages up to the year 2002 on employers paying full-time union officers and a ban on the occupation of workplaces during strikes.
The ICFTU said the ban on union membership for sacked employees "is a particularly serious violation because it acts as an incentive to discriminatory dismissal of union activists."

It would also exclude from the labour movement workers "who have already been victimised" including many members of the elected leadership of the KCTU who were "dismissed workers" and would not be eligible for union posts under the new law.
